domain_description: Where decades of learning-science research meets AI tools — intelligent tutoring systems, cognitive tutors, worked-example sequences, productive failure, AI-generated feedback, and the formative-assessment loops that hold it together. We curate hard here: the classical learning-science principles (Sweller, VanLehn, Kapur, Renkl, Black & Wiliam) have strong meta-analytic evidence; the AI-specific re-implementations often inherit that evidence, but not always — and where the AI angle outruns the research, we say so. TPACK is included as the framework teachers need to put any of this in motion.

skills.description: Design cognitive-tutor architecture — ACT-R cognitive model, knowledge-tracing of student state, mastery thresholds, step-level hints and error messages — so the tutor actually knows what the student knows and adapts, instead of just delivering branching worksheets.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Commercial cognitive tutors (Carnegie Learning, ALEKS) carry licence cost; building your own ACT-R-based tutor requires real cognitive-science engineering expertise. Either way, teacher PD is needed to integrate the tutor into classroom routines. Effect sizes are sensitive to comparison group and subject: Kulik & Fletcher's K-12 subsample sits at d=0.41 (vs d=0.66 overall), Steenbergen-Hu & Cooper 2013 found near-null effects in K-12 math vs classroom instruction (g=0.05), and a 2025 arXiv preprint on US K-12 reported g=0.27. The d=0.66 holds when the alternative is no tutoring or human tutoring — not necessarily strong classroom instruction.

skills.description: Design tutorial dialogue — step-based interaction, ICAP-aligned prompts (Interactive > Constructive > Active > Passive), mixed-initiative turns, and AutoTutor-style follow-up moves — so the tutor pulls reasoning out of the student instead of dumping explanations on them.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Dialogue tutors require real design work: dialogue-flow planning, ICAP-aligned prompting, mixed-initiative turn-taking, and follow-up move libraries. Classical ITS dialogue (AutoTutor, Cognitive Tutor) involves substantial engineering; LLM-based dialogue tutors lower the build cost but inherit the design principles. VanLehn's d=0.76 is for step-based dialogue vs no tutoring — answer-based interaction (just give the right answer) yields only d=0.31, so the cost is in making the dialogue actually step-based.

skills.description: Design hint hierarchies that fade from vague (point me at the right area) to specific (here's the next step), released only when the student is genuinely stuck, so the system supports productive struggle instead of bailing them out at the first wrong answer.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: No materials cost, but real design work: pedagogical analysis of common errors, a vague-to-specific hint hierarchy, and release conditions that wait for genuine stuck-ness rather than firing on the first wrong answer. Thomann & Deutscher's publication-bias-corrected effect drops to d=0.22, so the headline d=0.39 assumes well-designed prompts: concise, adaptive, and timed to the moment the student actually needs them. Aleven & colleagues' classic finding: 'help helps, but only so much' — over-hinting backfires.

skills.description: Design AI-generated feedback so it actually moves learning — specific, focused on the task and process (not the person), tied to clear criteria, and actionable. Built on Shute/Narciss/Hattie classical feedback principles, applied to LLM and automated-feedback systems.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: No materials cost. The lift is in knowing the classical feedback-design principles (Shute 2008, Narciss, Hattie) and translating them to AI prompts or system rules. AI feedback inherits the same constraints as human feedback: specific beats vague, task/process beats person, and uptake matters. Fleckenstein et al. found ~half of students make no revisions after receiving AI feedback — design has to push toward action, not just deliver a comment.

skills.description: Design problem-solving experiences that come before instruction — letting students grapple with a hard problem, generate partially-correct approaches, then receive instruction that consolidates what they have just struggled with. Kapur's PS-I (problem-solving followed by instruction), built on Bjork's desirable difficulties tradition.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: No materials cost. The real lift is on the teacher: designing a pre-instruction problem worth struggling on, tolerating visible student difficulty without bailing them out, and running a strong consolidation phase that converts the struggle into durable understanding. Sinha & Kapur found high-fidelity PS-I reaches g=0.37–0.58 — sloppy 'just let them struggle' implementations don't. Boundary conditions: stronger for older students and STEM topics; for grades 2–5 and domain-general skills, instruction-first (I-PS) actually outperformed PS-I.

skills.display_title: Worked Example to Problem Solving Transition Designer
skills.description: Design when and how to move students from studying worked examples to solving problems on their own — anchored in the expertise-reversal effect. Keep novices in high-assistance mode (full worked examples → completion problems → faded steps), move them to independent problem-solving as prior knowledge grows, and use diagnostic info to detect the crossover instead of assuming everyone is at the same place.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: No materials cost, but the skill needs diagnostic information about each learner's prior knowledge to decide when to fade — without that, you fade at the wrong time for half the class. Tetzlaff et al. (60 studies, 5,924 participants) found low-prior-knowledge learners gained d=0.51 from high-assistance instruction while high-prior-knowledge learners gained d=−0.43 from low-assistance instruction. The effect is asymmetrical: over-helping novices is worse than under-helping experts, so when uncertain, lean toward more scaffolding and fade conservatively. Effect is weaker for younger students and humanities/language learning.
